questions.question: Why do production Node services usually prefer structured JSON logs (e.g. pino) over console.log text lines?
options: console.log is not available in production builds
Each line has consistent, machine-searchable fields and a level, so logs can be filtered and aggregated across servers
JSON logs never need to be shipped anywhere
questions.explanation: Structured logs carry fields like level, requestId and orderId that log platforms can index, and levels let you turn debug noise off in production.

questions.question: A pino logger is created with level "info". What happens to `logger.debug("cache miss")`?
options: It is not written, because debug is below the configured info level
It is written as an info line
It is buffered and written on exit
questions.explanation: Only messages at or above the configured level are emitted. The level can be raised to debug through an env var like LOG_LEVEL when investigating.

questions.question: What does `node --inspect-brk script.js` do compared with `--inspect`?
options: It exposes the debugger on all network interfaces
It restarts the script when files change
It enables the inspector and pauses before the first line of user code runs
questions.explanation: --inspect-brk is useful for debugging start-up code, because execution waits until a debugger such as Chrome DevTools (via chrome://inspect) attaches and resumes.

questions.question: Why is running `node --inspect=0.0.0.0` on a public server dangerous?
options: It slows the event loop by 50%
Anyone who can reach the inspector port can execute arbitrary code in the process
It deletes logs on every restart
questions.explanation: The inspector protocol allows full code execution. It binds to 127.0.0.1 by default for this reason; never expose it publicly.
